text:
alex_support: Hey team — customer reports 502s when calling their private endpoint to our service via AWS PrivateLink. Works from one app subnet but fails from another. They say it was working yesterday.

sam_infra: Can you paste a curl -v output and the DNS resolution from the failing host? Also which VPC endpoint type (interface) and did they enable Private DNS?

alex_support: From customer: 
```
$ dig +short api.redwood.internal
10.0.12.45
10.0.13.22

$ curl -v https://api.redwood.internal/health
*   Trying 10.0.13.22:443...
* Connected to api.redwood.internal (10.0.13.22) port 443 (#0)
* ALPN, offering h2
* TLS 1.2 connection using TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
* server certificate verification OK
* SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'api.redwood.internal'
* Closing connection 0
curl: (51) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'api.redwood.internal'
```

jordan_network: That cert error is suspicious — looks like the endpoint IP is returning a cert for vpce-*.amazonaws.com or our public cert instead of the internal SAN. Two possible causes: (1) they resolve to the wrong hostname (private DNS not mapping the service name to the VPC endpoint DNS names) or (2) traffic is egressing to the public service IP (and hitting our public LB). But dig shows private IPs so probably endpoint ENI.

alex_support: Customer also ran `openssl s_client -connect 10.0.13.22:443 -servername api.redwood.internal -showcerts` and said the cert CN was `vpce-0a1b2c3d-abcdef.vpce-svc-xyz.region.vpce.amazonaws.com`.

sam_infra: Ok that confirms SNI served cert mismatch. We use SNI to serve customer-facing cert with api.redwood.internal in SAN only when the TLS flow hits our private endpoint service (and Private DNS is enabled). If the endpoint's private DNS isn't enabled or the endpoint was created against the wrong service name, the endpoint ENI may return the service endpoint cert. Two checks: 
1) On customer's account, ensure the Interface Endpoint has "Enable Private DNS Name" checked for the service name we provided.
2) Check the endpoint's security group — interface endpoints require the endpoint SG to allow inbound 443 from the client SG/CIDR. If the endpoint SG blocks, some middlebox could be bouncing; but not likely for cert mismatch.

jordan_network: Also ask them to run from failing subnet: `dig +short api.redwood.internal @10.0.0.2` (the VPC resolver) and `dig +short api.redwood.internal vpce-xxxx.region.vpce.amazonaws.com` to see whether the VPC resolver is translating the name to the vpce DNS or to ENI ips. If Private DNS is on, their name should resolve to the vpce DNS vended names which then map to ENI IPs but SNI should be api.redwood.internal.

alex_support: I asked for these outputs; customer pasted more: 
```
$ aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-endpoint-id,Values=vpce-0a1b2c3d --query 'VpcEndpoints[0].PrivateDnsEnabled' --output text
False

$ aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=description,Values='Interface endpoint for vpce-0a1b2c3d' --query 'NetworkInterfaces[*].PrivateIpAddress' --output text
10.0.12.45 10.0.13.22
```

sam_infra: Bingo — PrivateDnsEnabled=false. That means api.redwood.internal still resolves to our public ALB IPs for some hosts (or the client may have mixed resolution paths), and their app is bypassing the VPC endpoint host header mapping. The SNI/cert mismatch happens because traffic hits the VPN/IGW path to our public endpoint or the endpoint service returns the vpce cert when the Private DNS mapping isn't used.

jordan_network: Next steps for customer: enable Private DNS on the interface endpoint (or create an alias A records in a private hosted zone associated with their VPC) so api.redwood.internal resolves to the endpoint. If they can't enable it for some reason, they must use the vpce-specific DNS name in their requests and set SNI/Host header accordingly.

alex_support: They said they enabled it but only on one endpoint (in the working subnet) and forgot to enable on the endpoint in the failing subnet — they had one endpoint per AZ/subnet. Clarify: If they have multiple interface endpoints, each needs Private DNS or you can rely on a single endpoint per VPC with cross-AZ reachability, but we generally recommend one per AZ.

sam_infra: Also confirm security groups: run `aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --network-interface-ids eni-xxxx --query 'NetworkInterfaces[0].Groups'` and make sure the endpoint SG ingress allows the client SG on port 443. Quick check for SG rules that commonly block: endpoints created with a default SG that allows nothing.

alex_support: From customer: endpoint SG had only outbound rules, no ingress. They accidentally attached the wrong SG. After adding ingress rule allowing the app SG on TCP/443 the TLS error went away and requests succeeded. :tada:

jordan_network: Nice. For our internal notes: common checklist to send customers for PrivateLink issues: 
- Verify PrivateDnsEnabled on each interface endpoint.
- Verify Route53 private hosted zone association if they use PHZ mapping.
- Verify endpoint SG ingress allows client SG/CIDR on ports required (443).
- Check NACLs for overly strict rules on ENI subnets.
- Confirm SNI/Host header usage if using vpce-specific DNS names.
- If cross-account endpoint service, confirm acceptance and allowed principals on provider side.

alex_support: I'm going to reply with the exact commands and a short how-to to fix SG + private DNS. Also open a KB snippet we can paste for future. Thanks all.

deploy-bot: Reminder: added support-kb/privatelink-troubleshooting to backlog (ticket# 7892).

sam_infra: If you want I can draft the KB with the common aws cli commands and sample sg rules. Happy to take it.

alex_support: Please do. I'll follow up with the customer to confirm resolved and close the case.
